problems.location: Concept 2: Developmental Neurobiology and Dynamic Memory Systems / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Failure to retrieve a concept during a formal assessment reflects a mismatch in retrieval cues rather than an intrinsic absence of knowledge.
problems.source_text: Thus, if a person fails to remember a fact or skill at a particular time, that does not necessarily mean he does not possess the necessary knowledge.
problems.reason: The source says a failed recall does not necessarily mean the knowledge is missing, but the lesson says it always reflects a cue mismatch and never a lack of knowledge.

problems.location: Concept 2: Developmental Neurobiology and Dynamic Memory Systems / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Crucially, retrieving an existing memory destabilizes it, requiring **reconsolidation** that incorporates new contextual knowledge, current goals, and subsequent experiences.
problems.reason: Reconsolidation, meaning that retrieval destabilizes a memory, appears in none of the sources (searched How People Learn II for 'reconsolidat').

problems.location: Concept 2: Developmental Neurobiology and Dynamic Memory Systems / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Highly sensitive to initial encoding context and prone to systematic transformation across repeated reconsolidation cycles.
problems.reason: The episodic memory card adds a claim about reconsolidation cycles that the sources never make.

problems.location: Concept 2: Developmental Neurobiology and Dynamic Memory Systems / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Scaffolding maintains task accuracy until cognitive load exceeds available neural capacity, highlighting the need for self-paced learning.
problems.source_text: Older adults need to recruit those levels at a lower level of task difficulty than do younger adults.
problems.reason: The source's description of the CRUNCH model draws no conclusion about self-paced learning, so the lesson adds that implication on its own.

problems.location: Exercise 2.1: Deconstructing memory reconstruction and environmental cueing in adult skill retrieval / block 2
problems.lesson_text: The children’s recall is more context-dependent due to ongoing neuroplasticity and less consolidated episodic memory networks.
problems.reason: The model answer gives a causal claim that the sources never make: that children's recall depends more on context because of neuroplasticity.

problems.location: Concept 6: Evidence-Centered Instructional Design and Assessment / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Formative Feedback Loop
problems.source_text: Figure 7-1 illustrates the three essential components of the overall design process.
problems.reason: The source describes evidence-centered design as having three parts (claims, observation, tasks), but the lesson's table adds a fourth part, a formative feedback loop, plus a column of technology risks that the source does not have.

problems.location: Concept 4: Motivational Systems, Identity, and Self-Regulated Learning / block 1
problems.lesson_text: As synthesized by Carver & Scheier (2017) and Hattie & Donoghue (2016), effective self-regulation involves a cyclical loop of:
problems.source_text: they also highlighted important concepts such as forethought, performance control, self-reflection, cognition, and motivation. Regardless of the model, Moos and Ringdal (2012) suggested
problems.reason: The source credits the forethought, performance control and self-reflection framing to Moos and Ringdal (2012), not to Carver & Scheier or Hattie & Donoghue.

problems.location: Concept 4: Motivational Systems, Identity, and Self-Regulated Learning / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Surface memorization and rapid short-term recall; poor transfer
problems.source_text: However, research regarding the impact of performance goals on academic outcomes has yielded mixed findings (Elliot and McGregor, 2001; Midgley et al., 2001). Some researchers have found positive outcomes when learners have endorsed normative goals (a type of performance goal)
problems.reason: The source calls the evidence on performance goals mixed, with some positive results, while the lesson says flatly that performance-approach goals lead to poor outcomes.

problems.location: Concept 5: The Functional and Ethical Spectrum of AI in Education / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Making & Helping (Generative Tools)
problems.source_text: Helping Works alongside a task to make it easier. ... For example: captions under a lecture, a menu translated at the table, a screen reader keeping pace with the page. Sometimes AI makes a task easier. Sometimes it’s what makes the task possible at all.
problems.reason: Compass describes Helping as support tools such as captions and screen readers, but the lesson recasts it as a generative tool that drafts text and code, with cognitive atrophy as its main risk.

problems.location: Concept 5: The Functional and Ethical Spectrum of AI in Education / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Invisible AI tools do not announce their presence; students and educators simply encounter their consequences. When predictive analytics tag a learner as 'at risk' or route them to remedial tracks, institutional systems risk creating self-fulfilling feedback loops.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. ... Invisible doesn’t mean sinister. Most of what’s on this list is useful, and some of it is the reason a person can take part at all.
problems.reason: The lesson presents invisible AI mainly as a governance risk, while Compass stresses that none of these tools is good or bad on its own and that what matters is whether someone chose the tool on purpose and whether the person affected knew.

problems.location: Concept 1: Situated Learning and Workplace Learning Ecologies / block 5
problems.lesson_text: In robust workplace learning, digital platforms and AI tools serve as connective nodes that scaffold practice and amplify human interaction
problems.source_text: Learning in the flow of work means learning through real work, with other people, not just getting answers at the moment of need.
problems.reason: The lesson never warns against the predictable mistake the slides address, treating instant AI answers at the moment of need as learning in the flow of work; its Self-Paced card even frames learning as filling 'a specific factual gap'.

problems.location: Concept 2: Developmental Neurobiology and Dynamic Memory Systems / block 5
problems.lesson_text: Educational leaders and instructional designers must recognize that a single isolated assessment measures cue compatibility and contextual performance at one snapshot in time, rather than a permanent ceiling on a learner's cognitive capability.
problems.reason: Block 3 of the same concept already explained that "Failure to retrieve a concept during a formal assessment reflects a mismatch in retrieval cues rather than an intrinsic absence of knowledge", and this callout explains the same point again in new words instead of building on it.

problems.location: Concept 3: Knowledge Architecture, Inferential Reasoning, and Conceptual Models / block 1
problems.lesson_text: Neurocognitive evidence reveals that this occurs through the continuous reactivation and reconsolidation of memory traces: when new information overlaps with prior elements, the brain establishes relational links that transform individual episodes into generalized semantic structures.
problems.reason: Concept 2 already explained reconsolidation (block 3) and how relational binding links features and how semantic memory is abstracted away from specific episodes (block 4), and this sentence explains that process again as new evidence without pointing back to Concept 2.

problems.location: Concept 3: Knowledge Architecture, Inferential Reasoning, and Conceptual Models / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Infers underlying causal structures or explanatory processes from incomplete data.
problems.reason: The table defines abductive, inductive and deductive reasoning and model-based simulation again (with the same geometry-theorem and thermostat and flat-disk examples), although block 1 of the same concept had just defined each of them.

problems.location: Concept 5: The Functional and Ethical Spectrum of AI in Education / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Invisible AI tools do not announce their presence; students and educators simply encounter their consequences.
problems.reason: Block 1 already explained that with invisible AI learners and instructors "simply encounter the systemic consequences of its decisions", and block 2 already gave the labeling risk, so the callout explains both points again instead of only adding the feedback-loop idea.

problems.location: Concept 6: Evidence-Centered Instructional Design and Assessment / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Mixing contrasting case problems to train learners in structural discrimination and adaptive selection of mathematical or diagnostic procedures.
problems.reason: Three of the four cards (spaced retrieval, interleaving, generative explanation) explain again the strategies block 1 had just explained, for example block 1 already said interleaving "trains learners to identify deep structural differences and select appropriate strategies".

problems.location: Concept 6: Evidence-Centered Instructional Design and Assessment / block 4
problems.lesson_text: When appraising instructional software, curriculum designs, or digital platforms, education leaders must evaluate whether the tool builds an internal cognitive capacity or silently replaces it.
problems.reason: Concept 5 block 4 already explained the adopt, adapt or reject lens of capacity building versus cognitive replacement and learner agency, and this callout explains the same lens again in a different concept without pointing back to it.
